To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
microbial transport in streams is highly variable, with microbes being retained in streambed sediments and in submerged macrophytes and with microbial inactivation rates being highly variable.

(1) we developed a stochastic modeling framework that can be used to assess microbial transport, retention, inactivation, and survival in streams; (2) the model is capable of predicting microbial transport and survival in streams with reasonable accuracy, and (3), microbial inactivation is important for predicting microbial survival in streams.

microbial inactivation processes are important in streams and need to be considered in microbial transport models and that a combination of laboratory, field, and model studies are required to better understand microbial dynamics in streams.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of new tools to improve understanding and prediction of microbial transport in rivers and streams.
the fate and transport of microbial contaminants in rivers.
understanding how microbial pathogens move and are inactivated in streams.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the combined experimental and stochastic modeling approach can improve our ability to predict the fate of pathogenic microbes in streams.

this study advances the state of knowledge of microbial transport and inactivation in streams by providing (1) improved experimental data, (2) improved stochastic model structure to account for inactivation, and (3 ) improved model parameters to better represent the microbial processes that are important in streams.
microbial transport and inactivation in streams are highly dynamic processes that can be described with a stochastic model that includes the relevant microbial processes.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the combination of field tracer experiments, laboratory experiments, and stochastic transport models can be used to assess microbial transport and retention in streams and that microbial inactivation is an important process to consider in these systems.
microbial transport and retention dynamics are complex, but can be modeled using a multiscale stochastic approach that includes inactivation processes.

we have improved our understanding of microbial transport, retention, inactivation and their seasonal dynamics, and we have developed a stochastic model that can be used to better predict how microbial transport varies with environmental conditions and stream morphology.
The main takeaway from our work is that

we have demonstrated a framework to assess how microbial inactivation processes affect microbial fate in streams, which is a critical step in understanding the role of streams in the transmission of waterborne diseases.
we need to improve understanding of how microorganisms are retained and transported in freshwater systems to better predict how water-borne pathogens are transmitted.
the combination of experiments and modeling provides a new framework to assess microbial dynamics in streams and to better predict microbial transport and inactivation processes in streams.
